column2: No one is an enemy or friend of anyone by nature; by cause enemy and friend. This twelve-king circle has been told to you.
Enemies are to be known as of three kinds: kinsman, next-neighbor and artificial; the earlier one is the heavier, held hardest to cure.
Even the next-door enemy is considered artificial by me. The Parshnigraha would be the enemy's friends and enemies likewise;
one should pacify the Parshnigraha by means, and likewise one's own. The ancients praise the uprooting of the enemy through a friend;
and a friend becomes an enemy by being next-neighbor. The conqueror should uproot the enemy himself, if he is able;
when his might has grown, fear does not come from a non-friend either. So that the people are not distressed and trust arises,
the conqueror, victorious by dharma, should bring the people under control.
Peace, war, march, halt, dual policy and seeking refuge — the six measures are declared.
Peace is remembered as a bond by stake; war is injury; the conqueror's march into the enemy's region is called yana;
staying in one's own country while at war is called asana; marching with half the force is called dvaidhibhava;
taking refuge with a neutral or middle king is called samshraya. Peace should be sought with an equal, and with a stronger one not inferior;
war should be made by the king himself with an inferior; and with a stronger one, one whose rear is clean should take refuge.
When one sitting is able to cut off the enemy's operations, one with unclean rear should sit, after making war, the lord of the earth;
the strong with an unclean rear should resort to the dual policy. The king who is attacked by a strong one without doubt
should resort to refuge — the lowest of the measures. Their march involves much loss, expense and effort;
then afterward, bringing much gain, the king should take it up; one deprived of all power should then seek refuge.
Staying there he should see Brahmins, ministers and counselors, and the subjects, great one, announced by the door-keeper;
having heard history, tasks and decision of the tasks, he should then see to legal business; he should take counsel with counselors.
He should not take counsel with one alone, nor with many, nor with fools or the untrustworthy; he should act secretly, not openly;
he should make the counsel well established so that the nation is not harmed. In the matter of reading the king's expressions, protection of counsel is held supreme;
the wise grasp counsel by expressions and hints with intelligence. The king who is attentive to the words of astrologers, physicians and counselors
obtains prosperity, for they support the king. Having taken counsel, then exercise, in vehicle and weapons,
the king, bathed, seeing Vishnu well worshipped, should see the oblation-fire and see well-honored Brahmins;
adorned he should take food, well tested, by gifts and the rest; having eaten, taking betel, resting on the left side,
he should think of scriptures; having seen warriors, the armory and the house; having attended the evening twilight and thought about the tasks,
having sent out spies, having eaten, he should be a frequenter of the inner palace; guarded with music and songs and others, the king should thus always conduct himself.
Tell me what is desired and undesired in the dream of the one sleeping, eternal one. The priest should utter the mantra "yaj jagrato dura";
on the third day one should worship the world-guardians, the Rudras, the lords of directions; on the fourth day one should worship the planets, on the fifth the Ashvins;
worship of the deities on the road and of rivers and the like, and likewise offerings to the gods dwelling in heaven, sky and earth;
at night worship of the hosts of beings, Vasudeva and the rest; one should perform for Bhadrakali and Shri; one should pray to all gods:
Vasudeva, Sankarshana, Pradyumna and Aniruddha, Narayana, the lotus-born, Vishnu, Narasimha, Varaha,
Shiva, Isha, Tatpurusha, Aghora, Rama, Satyaja; Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn,
Rahu, Ketu, Ganapati, the Commander, Chandika and Uma, Lakshmi, Sarasvati, Durga, the hosts headed by Brahmani,
Rudras, Indra and the rest, Fire, nagas, Garuda, other gods — may those dwelling in heaven, sky and earth be for my victory.

May they crush the enemies in battle, accepting the offering. I, with son, mother and servants, have gone to you gods for refuge.
agnipuran:234:14	Having gone behind the armies, homage to you, destroyers of enemies. Returning, I shall give an offering greater than what is given.
On the sixth day the victory bath should be done like a consecration. On the seventh day of the journey one should worship Trivikrama;
with the mantras stated in the lustration one should worship weapon and vehicle; with the sound of auspicious day and victory one should listen to this mantra:

May the gods dwelling in heaven, sky and earth be givers of life to you; obtain success of the gods; may that be your divine journey.
agnipuran:234:18	May all deities protect — hearing this the king should go. Taking the bow with arrow, with the mantra "dhanur naga,"
having recited "tad vishnoh," he should place his foot on the enemy's face; the right foot in thirty-two directions in order beginning with the east;
he should mount in order elephant, chariot, horse and draught animals. Having mounted, he should go with music, not looking behind;
having gone a krosha he should stop and worship the deities and Brahmins. Afterward he should go to the enemy country protecting his own army.
The king, having reached the lord of gods, should protect the country-guardian; he should worship the gods and not cut the revenue there;
he should not insult the people of that country; having come again to his own city, having obtained victory, the king should worship the gods and give gifts.
When on the second day a battle will take place, then one should bathe elephant, horse and the rest, and worship the god Nripasimha;
the umbrella and other royal insignia, weapons at night, and the hosts; in the morning having worshipped Narasimha, vehicles and the rest entirely,
he should see the fire oblation done by the priest; having offered, worship Brahmins; taking bow with arrows, mounting an elephant and the rest, he should go.
In the country, unseen by enemies, he should arrange the constituents; he should make a few fight in a compact body, spread the many as desired.
An army for a few with many would be needle-faced. Formations are declared in the form of animal limbs and of objects:
Garuda, Makara formation, Wheel, Hawk likewise, Half-moon, Thunderbolt, and Cart formation,
Circle, All-auspicious, and Needle formation — those men. For all formations the army arrangement is fivefold:
two wings, two supporting wings, and a fifth, the reserve; one should fight with one or two parts;
three parts one should station for their protection. The king should never be made part of the formation;
if the root is cut, destruction results; the king should not fight himself. The king should stay a krosha behind the army;
there the rallying of the broken warriors is declared; when the chief is broken the army meets its place of destruction.
One should not arrange warriors in a formation too close or too sparse, so that weapons do not crowd one another;
one wishing to break the enemy's force should break with compact ones; those protected from breaking should be kept compact by the enemy too.
One should make a formation that breaks others' formations at will. Four men for protecting an elephant's feet, twice-born,
and four horses for a chariot; equal to it are those with shields; archers equal to shield-bearers; in battle shield-bearers in front,
archers behind, horses behind archers, chariots; behind chariots elephants should be placed by the king.
The duty of infantry, elephants and horses is to be carried out with effort. Brave ones should be placed in front, showing only shoulder;
the troop of the timid should do what makes the enemy flee; those who tear in front, the timid should not be placed in front;
the brave standing in front encourage the timid in battle. Tall men, those who see omens and those of straight gaze,
with brows joined, angry, fond of quarrels, ever glad and exultant, are to be known as brave, and the amorous.
The act of removing the compact and the slain from the battle, counter-fighting of elephants and the giving of water and the like,
fetching weapons, is ordained as infantry work; protecting one's own army from enemies wishing to break it,
and breaking the compact, is declared the shield-bearers' work; turning away in battle is likewise said of archers;
retreat far and transport for the well-slain is said; terrifying the enemy army is said to be chariot work;
breaking the compact and rejoining the broken; breaking ramparts, gates, watchtowers and trees in an encounter.
The ground for infantry is to be known as uneven, for chariot and horse level, and for elephants muddy: so the battlefield is declared.
Thus with the formation arranged, the sun at his back, and favorable Venus, sun, direction-guardians and gentle wind,
one should rouse all warriors by names, clans and deeds: with enjoyment obtained in victory and heaven obtained for the dead;
having conquered enemies, enjoyment is gained; for the dead, the supreme goal. Repayment of the master's rice: there is no goal equal to battle.
The blood of the brave comes forth; by it they abandon sin. Enduring the pain of wounds and the like in battle is the supreme austerity.
